opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the clearest way to frame it is that the constraints are different, and constraints shape culture.

In the West, especially at the big labs like OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and Meta, the default assumption for years was that compute would keep showing up. You could raise more money, sign another cloud deal, and get another cluster of the latest Nvidia chips. So the optimization culture there often looks like "how do we use this enormous pile of GPUs well at scale?" It's real engineering, and there's lots of it, but the bottleneck people feel day to day is often research direction, data, or organizational speed, not whether they can squeeze another 10% out of a kernel.

In China it's a different situation. Export controls mean that teams like DeepSeek, Qwen at Alibaba, Moonshot, and others are working with restricted hardware, like the H800s or H20s, or with domestic chips that have less mature software stacks. When you can't simply buy your way to more compute, the infrastructure and optimization layer stops being a support function and becomes core research. DeepSeek is the canonical example. Things like their mixture-of-experts design choices, multi-head latent attention to shrink the KV cache, FP8 training, custom communication kernels to work around interconnect bandwidth limits, even dropping below CUDA to PTX in places. That is a team where the systems people and the modeling people are basically the same people, co-designing the model around the hardware.

The other piece is openness. A lot of the Chinese labs publish these infrastructure details and release weights, and DeepSeek even open-sourced pieces of their training and inference stack. Western frontier labs tend to treat that layer as a competitive moat and say very little. So paradoxically, a lot of what the open research community knows about efficient frontier-scale training right now comes from Chinese technical reports.

I'd add a caveat, though. It's easy to over-romanticize the "scrappy efficiency" story. The top Western labs are extremely good at infrastructure too; they just don't write about it, and their efficiency gains get reinvested into bigger runs rather than headlines about cheap training. And the Chinese labs would absolutely take more compute if they could get it. Efficiency is partly a virtue and partly a necessity.

So my short answer is that Western labs optimize to scale further, and Chinese labs optimize to stay in the game under constraints. Both approaches are converging on similar techniques, but the incentives that got them there are pretty different, and that shows up in how openly they share the work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to frame it is that the two ecosystems are optimizing under very different constraints, and that shapes where the engineering effort goes.

In the US, the frontier labs have historically been compute-rich. When you have tens of thousands of the latest Nvidia chips, the rational thing to do is spend your best people on the research and the model, and treat infrastructure as something you buy and scale. You still do a ton of systems work, but the pressure to squeeze every last FLOP out of a given chip just isn't as intense. The marginal gain from a clever kernel is small relative to the marginal gain from just getting more hardware online.

The Chinese labs, especially after the export controls tightened, have been living in a world where compute is the binding constraint. So you see this really deep investment in the layer between the model and the silicon. DeepSeek is the obvious example. A lot of what made their training runs remarkable wasn't a new architecture idea in isolation, it was things like writing custom communication schedules, going below CUDA to PTX for certain operations, mixed-precision training with FP8 done very carefully, and co-designing the MoE routing with the actual network topology they had. That's the kind of work you do when you can't just ask for more GPUs.

And I think there's a cultural piece too. Several of these labs came out of quant finance or very engineering-driven organizations, where low-latency systems work is prestigious. In a lot of Western labs the status hierarchy puts the research scientist at the top and the infrastructure engineer one tier down, even though everyone knows the infra is what makes the runs actually happen.

The other thing I'd flag is that the Chinese side has been much more willing to publish the details. The DeepSeek-V3 tech report reads like a systems paper as much as an ML paper. Western labs have largely stopped disclosing that layer, partly for competitive reasons and partly because it's just not where they think their edge is.

Now, the caveat is that this gap closes in both directions. As US labs scale to hundreds of thousands of chips, the efficiency problems become unavoidable and they end up doing the same optimization work, just later. And as Chinese labs get access to domestic accelerators like Huawei's Ascend, they have to rebuild a lot of that software stack from scratch, which is painful. So it's less a permanent philosophical difference and more a question of which constraint is biting hardest at a given moment.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is less about China versus the West in some fundamental sense and more about the constraints each company is operating under. If you have relatively abundant access to compute, you can prioritize moving quickly: train a bigger model, run more experiments, and accept some inefficiency along the way. If compute is harder to get, you have a stronger incentive to make the infrastructure and optimization work really well.

That optimization layer is everything between the model architecture and the hardware: how you distribute training, how you move data around, how efficiently you use memory, and how much useful computation you get out of each chip. It’s not necessarily visible to someone using the chatbot, but it can make a huge difference in the cost of training and serving it.

So my impression is that some Chinese labs have a particularly strong incentive to invest there and treat efficiency as a core research problem. But I wouldn’t make that a blanket distinction. Western labs also do an enormous amount of systems optimization. The interesting question is where each organization puts its next unit of effort: into acquiring more compute, or into getting more out of the compute it already has.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is where the constraints are, and therefore where companies have an incentive to optimize. For Chinese AI companies, access to compute is a much more explicit constraint. That puts pressure on the whole stack: how efficiently you train, how you move data between GPUs, how much memory you use, and how cheaply you can serve the model. Infrastructure becomes very closely connected to the model design.

The leading Western labs care enormously about efficiency too, but they’ve generally had more room to pursue scale—to buy more compute and build bigger clusters. So the question can be, “How do we get the best possible model with this enormous infrastructure investment?” Whereas a company operating under tighter constraints might start with, “How do we get comparable capability with the hardware we can actually access?”

I wouldn’t make that a hard distinction between China and the West. There’s substantial variation within both. But constraints can drive very good engineering, and that’s why I’d be careful about treating access to more chips as the same thing as having an insurmountable advantage. The software and optimization layer determines how much useful capability you actually get out of those chips.
